title: Choosing marketing channels and measuring them
audience: Any home-service operator choosing where to spend a marketing budget.
learningOutcomes: Compare at least three marketing channels using cost, reach to the chosen segment and expected response
Calculate cost per new customer for each channel from a supplied log
Set up a way to tag each new customer with the channel that brought them

instruction.heading: Match channels to the segment
instruction.body: A channel is a route to a segment: a printed brochure, a partner group, a referral, a directory listing, a local newspaper section or a website. Start from the segment profile written in “Defining target segments from customer data” and ask where that group already pays attention. A channel that reaches many people outside the segment costs money without adding customers. The sample plan this lesson draws on used three routes: a colour brochure placed through clubs whose members fit its target profile, a referral incentive, and an advertising campaign in the weekly home section of two local newspapers. Those choices suited a United States residential cleaner in the early 2000s. Local business networks and referral groups are another route to test. Some councils publish directories of them, so search your own council's listings. A Victorian council directory is one example. Before you copy any route, test whether it reaches your segment in your own area today.

instruction.heading: Compare channels on the same basis
instruction.body: Put every channel in one table with the same columns: the cost to run it for a set period, the number of people in the segment it reaches, the expected response rate, the expected number of new customers, and the time until the first job. Expected figures are estimates, so write down how each one was made, so you can check it later. Then shortlist the one or two channels with the lowest expected cost per new customer that still reach the segment, and test them with a fixed budget before committing the full amount.

instruction.heading: Measure cost per new customer
instruction.body: The main test of a channel is its cost per new customer. Divide the total cost of the channel in a period by the number of new customers who arrived through it in that period. Compare that figure with what a new customer is worth to you, using the average first-year value of a customer from your own records. A channel that costs more per customer than a customer is worth loses money, even when it produces many enquiries.

instruction.heading: Tag every enquiry
instruction.body: A channel can only be measured if each enquiry is tagged. Ask every new customer at booking how they heard about you, and record the answer against a fixed list such as brochure, club, referral, newspaper, website or other. Keep the other category small and review it each month. Unexplained budget lines hide the same problem. The sample plan put most of its budget into a single line labelled only other, so that line could not be judged until it was broken into named activities. The plan's amounts are removed here because they are United States figures.

instruction.heading: Set a target and review on a fixed date
instruction.body: Set a target for each measure, such as a maximum cost per new customer, and review the channel table on a fixed day each month. The sample plan set a marketing objective for reducing its customer acquisition cost each year. That was an early 2000s United States target, and its size is removed here. Use the wording only: a direction, a size and a period. Each review should end with a decision for each channel: keep, change or stop, recorded with its reason.

procedure: List the segments from “Defining target segments from customer data” and the channels you could use for each.
For each channel, estimate the cost for a set period, the reach, the expected response and the expected new customers, and note how each estimate was made.
Test the one or two channels with the lowest expected cost per customer, using a fixed budget for a set period.
Tag every enquiry with its channel at the time of booking.
Divide each channel's cost by its new paying customers for each month.
Review the table on a fixed date, decide to keep, change or stop each channel, and record the decision.

workedExamples.situation: A bathroom and kitchen cleaning business (hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson) runs a local flyer costing $240 AUD a month and a referral reward costing $120 AUD a month. Over three months the flyer brings 2 new customers and the referral brings 4.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which channel should receive next month's budget, and what should be checked before that decision is made?
workedExamples.reasoning: Flyer cost per new customer is $360 AUD ($720 AUD divided by 2). Referral cost per new customer is $90 AUD ($360 AUD divided by 4). On this test the referral is cheaper per customer. Before scaling it, check that the referral customers were tagged correctly, that four customers is enough to trust the result, and that the average first-year value of a customer is well above $90 AUD.

equipmentAndPpe: Booking form with a channel question

commonErrors.error: Judging a channel by the number of enquiries alone
commonErrors.prevention: Divide cost by new paying customers, and compare the result with the first-year value of a customer.

commonErrors.error: Spending the whole budget on one untested channel
commonErrors.prevention: Test each channel for a fixed period with a fixed budget before scaling it up.
Make the source question compulsory on the booking form and review any blanks each month.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Marketing sent by email, text or other electronic message is regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). The ACMA guidance summarised in the officialReferences says it needs consent, sender identification and a working unsubscribe. That guidance is a summary and not the Act text, so check the current Act and ACMA wording before any electronic campaign. See “Referral incentives that respect consumer and spam rules” and the source references.
Letterbox and door-drop distribution may be restricted by local council rules or by no-junk-mail signage at premises. Check the rules for the council area where you distribute.

qualityStandard: Each channel has a stated cost, expected response and cost per new customer.
Every new customer record carries a channel tag.
documentationEvidence: Channel comparison table with the basis for each estimate
Monthly log of spend and new customers by channel
Review notes recording the keep, change or stop decision for each channel
summary: Choose channels that reach the segment you defined in “Defining target segments from customer data”.
Cost per new customer is the main test of a channel.
Tag every enquiry so results can be compared.

knowledgeChecks.question: A channel costs $600 AUD and brings 4 new customers. What is the cost per new customer?
Which measure shows whether a marketing channel was worth what it cost?
options: The number of brochures printed and their colour and size
Cost per new customer compared with the value of a customer
The number of social media followers and the number of likes
The hours the owner spent on the channel and the design time

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should every new booking record how the customer heard about the business?
options: To make the booking form longer and to add more questions for the team
To tag each new customer to a channel so the results can be compared
To avoid collecting contact details and to keep the records private
To replace the need for a cost record for each channel

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: ACMA guidance on the Spam Act 2003: consent is required before marketing messages, and keeping a record of express consent is advised; inferred consent is less reliable than express consent; the sender must be identified accurately with correct contact details kept for at least 30 days; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option that is clear, free, needs no account or extra personal information, and works for at least 30 days; unsubscribe requests must be honoured within 5 working days. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA). This is a summary of the guidance, not the Act text, which was not read.
